summary: Specifies an option for the IP header that lets a datagram collect timestamps as it travels, so you can see when it passed through each point. It is a measurement aid for the Internet Protocol.

eli5.summary: Like asking every post office a package visits to stamp the time on it, this lets a packet carry a trail of clock readings from its trip.

questions: how do routers measure network delay
subtitle: Adding clock timestamps to IP packets to measure network delays.

tldr.problem: Network engineers needed to measure the time delay as packets traveled through interconnected networks (catenets), but had no standard way to collect timing data.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an IP header option that lets routers and gateways stamp the current time into a packet as it passes through, creating a trail of clock readings along the packet's path.
tldr.outcome: This allows operators to measure end-to-end delays and delays across individual networks by examining the sequence of timestamps in a packet that reaches its destination.

facts.label: Time unit
facts.value: Milliseconds modulo 24 hours from midnight UT

today: The IP timestamp option is defined in RFC 791 (the standard IP specification) but is rarely used in modern networks. Delays are typically measured using dedicated tools like ICMP traceroute or specialized monitoring protocols.

sections.title: Measuring Network Delay
sections.content:
As networks became interconnected via gateways into larger catenets, measuring the delay experienced by packets became important for understanding performance. The RFC defines an IP timestamp option that allows gateways to record the time when each packet passes through them.

Measurement requires that device clocks be synchronized, using facilities such as WWVB time service. The timestamp is a 32-bit value representing milliseconds modulo 24 hours from midnight UT.
sections.eli5: When a packet travels through the network, each router can write down what time it saw it. By collecting all these times, you can figure out how long the packet took.

sections.title: The Timestamp Option
sections.content:
The option type is 68 (decimal), with a maximum length of 40 octets. The format includes an offset field (the byte count to the end of timestamps), an overflow counter (devices that could not stamp due to lack of space), and a flags field controlling the mode:

  • Flag 0: timestamps only
  • Flag 1: each timestamp is preceded by the Internet ID of the router
  • Flag 3: the Internet ID fields are pre-specified; routers only stamp if they match the next expected ID

When the offset becomes odd (indicating no more room for timestamps), no additional routers can add timestamps. The option is carried in the first fragment of a fragmented packet.
sections.eli5: The timestamp field is like a logbook with limited pages. Each router writes its ID and the time, then passes it on. If the book gets full, later routers skip it and mark how many could not fit.

sections.title: Using Timestamps for Delay Measurement
sections.content:
To measure one-way delay, the originating host sends a packet with the timestamp option, and the destination examines the sequence of timestamps collected. The difference between consecutive timestamps shows the delay across that segment of the network.

Applications can use test packets specifically for measurement, or can piggyback timestamps on user traffic. Because the timestamp option is an IP-level option, gateways impose minimal additional overhead compared to handling normal packets.
sections.eli5: Each timestamp shows when the packet left that location. By comparing times, you can see how long the packet spent on each hop of its journey.
